hints: Recall what you observe when testing Group 2 hydroxides with water, from almost insoluble magnesium hydroxide to quite soluble barium hydroxide, to state the direction of the trend.
Think of dissolving as a two stage energy cycle, breaking the lattice apart then hydrating the separated ions, and name those two enthalpy changes.
Consider how increasing cation size down the group affects attraction to anions in the solid versus attraction to water molecules, and which ion size stays constant.
Link the overall balance of those two enthalpy changes to whether dissolving becomes more or less favourable down the group.
walkthrough:
Picture the observed trend**
Think of the hydroxides side by side in water. $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is almost insoluble, it forms the milky suspension in milk of magnesia. $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ is sparingly soluble limewater, while $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$ and $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ dissolve much more readily to give strongly alkaline solutions. So solubility clearly increases going down Group 2.

Split dissolving into two energy steps**
Imagine dissolving $\text{M(OH)}_2$ in terms of energy. First you must pull the lattice apart into gaseous ions, which costs energy equal and opposite to lattice enthalpy. Then you surround the gaseous $\text{M}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ ions with water, which releases hydration enthalpy: $$\Delta H_{sol} = -\Delta H_{latt} + \Delta H_{hyd}$$ Both $\Delta H_{latt}$ and $\Delta H_{hyd}$ are exothermic for ion formation and hydration, so you need to see how each changes with cation size.

See why both enthalpies become less exothermic**
Down the group $\text{M}^{2+}$ gets larger: $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is small, $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is large. A larger cation has lower charge density, so it attracts $\text{OH}^{-}$ ions in the lattice less strongly and it also attracts water molecules less strongly. That means breaking the lattice costs less energy, and hydrating the cation releases less energy. So both $\Delta H_{latt}$ and $\Delta H_{hyd}$ become less negative.

Decide which effect wins**
Here is the key A Level insight. The $\text{OH}^{-}$ ion is very small and its size does not change. Lattice enthalpy depends on the sum of cation plus anion radii, so when the cation is small like $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, the lattice is very strong, and when the cation grows the lattice strength falls sharply. Hydration of the large $\text{OH}^{-}$ ion changes very little, and even cation hydration falls less steeply than lattice enthalpy. Because $\Delta H_{latt}$ falls faster, the overall $\Delta H_{sol}$ becomes more exothermic down the group, making dissolving more favourable and solubility increase.

Final answer: Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group.
Both $\Delta H_{latt}$ and $\Delta H_{hyd}$ of $\text{M}^{2+}$ become less exothermic / less negative down the group as ionic radius increases.
$\Delta H_{latt}$ decreases more rapidly than $\Delta H_{hyd}$ because $\text{OH}^{-}$ is small compared to $\text{M}^{2+}$, so lattice enthalpy is dominated by the change in cation size.
Therefore $\Delta H_{sol}$ becomes more exothermic / more negative down the group, favouring greater solubility.

hints: Compare the sizes of $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ and think about which has the higher charge density and greater distorting power.
Think about what happens to the $\text{O-H}$ bond in $\text{OH}^{-}$ when the cation pulls strongly on the electrons, and how that helps form the oxide and water.
walkthrough:
Compare the two cations**
Both cations carry the same $2+$ charge, so size decides everything. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is much smaller than $\text{Sr}^{2+}$, so its charge is packed into a tiny volume. That gives $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ a far higher charge density and much stronger polarising power. So you can already predict $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ will be the less thermally stable one.

See how polarisation breaks the hydroxide**
Picture $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ sitting next to $\text{OH}^{-}$ in the solid: $$\text{M(OH)}_2(s) \rightarrow \text{MO}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$$ The small $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ pulls electron density out of the $\text{OH}^{-}$ ion and distorts it strongly. This weakens the $\text{O-H}$ bond and makes it much easier to split $\text{OH}^{-}$ to form $\text{O}^{2-}$ in the oxide plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Less heat is needed, so $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ decomposes at a lower temperature than $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$.

Final answer: $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ decomposes at a lower temperature.
$\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is smaller than $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ / has higher charge density and greater polarising power.
It polarises / distorts the $\text{OH}^{-}$ ion more, weakening the $\text{O-H}$ bond so decomposition to the oxide occurs more easily.
